title: One GET, End to End: What Requests Promises and Where It Trusts You
premise: A caller has a URL and a pair of credentials: `requests.get('http://127.0.0.1:54897/basic-auth/user/pass', auth=('user','pass'))`. Between that line and a parsed JSON dict lies every decision Requests makes on your behalf — which headers it adds, whether it checks a certificate, how long it will wait, where it will send your password next, and what it does with a response body it has not yet read. This story follows that URL and that password through the library, stopping wherever a guarantee is made or a default quietly decides something for you.

chapters.title: A URL and a Password Walk Into a Session
chapters.data_out: the same url/auth, now inside a live Session: headers {'User-Agent': 'python-requests/2.34.2', 'Accept-Encoding': 'gzip, deflate', 'Accept': '*/*', 'Connection': 'keep-alive'}, empty RequestsCookieJar, HTTPAdapters mounted at 'https://' and 'http://'
facts: The module-level `requests.get` builds a brand-new Session inside a `with` block, so the session (and its sockets) is closed when the call returns \u2014 no connection reuse between successive `requests.get` calls.
Session defaults set here decide the rest of the story: `verify=True`, `stream=False`, `trust_env=True`, `max_redirects=30` (DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LIMIT), `auth=None`, `proxies={}`.
`HTTPAdapter.__init__` with the default `max_retries=0` builds `Retry(0, read=False)`: Requests does not retry anything by default, including connection failures.
Four headers are added unconditionally on every request, including a `User-Agent` that identifies the library and version ('python-requests/2.34.2').
Only 'http://' and 'https://' are mounted; any other scheme has no transport at all.

open_questions.question: Nothing here looked at a certificate. Who finally decides whether the server's TLS identity is checked, and what is the default?
This Session exists for exactly one request. What is gained and what is given up by throwing it away?

chapters.title: Merging What the Caller Said With What the Session Believes
chapters.data_in: Session.request(method='get', url=..., auth=('user','pass'), everything else None)
chapters.data_out: a Request [GET] plus merged settings: headers CaseInsensitiveDict with the four defaults, params OrderedDict(), auth ('user','pass'), cookies <RequestsCookieJar[]>, hooks {'response': []}
facts: `merge_setting` gives per-request values precedence over session values for dict-like settings, and a per-request key set to `None` *deletes* the session's key \u2014 the documented way to suppress a session default.
Non-dict settings (verify, stream, cert) bypass merging entirely: the request value wins outright if it is not None.

Because an explicit `auth` tuple was supplied, the `get_netrc_auth(url)` branch was skipped. Had `auth` been None and `trust_env` True, credentials from `~/.netrc` would have been injected silently \u2014 and netrc auth overrides an Authorization header the caller set via `headers=`.
Session cookies are merged into a fresh RequestsCookieJar for this request; the session's own jar is not mutated at preparation time.
The method string is upper-cased twice (once in `Session.request`, once in `prepare_request`) \u2014 'get' and 'GET' are equivalent inputs.

open_questions.question: The credentials are still just a Python tuple. When and how do they become something that goes on the wire?

chapters.title: Turning a String Into a URL You Can Trust
facts: `prepare` runs a fixed order \u2014 method, url, headers, cookies, body, auth, hooks \u2014 and the comments make the ordering a contract: auth must be able to see a fully built request, and hooks must be registered after auth.

Roads not taken, all raising before any socket opens: no scheme \u2192 `MissingSchema`; no host \u2192 `InvalidURL`; a host starting with '*' or '.' \u2192 `InvalidURL('URL has an invalid label.')`; a urllib3 `LocationParseError` \u2192 `InvalidURL`.

A URL containing ':' that does not start with 'http' (e.g. `mailto:`, `data:`) is stored *verbatim* with no parsing or validation \u2014 a deliberate escape hatch that later fails at adapter selection instead.
Non-ASCII hostnames are IDNA-encoded via the `idna` package; here `unicode_is_ascii('127.0.0.1')` was True so the host passed through unchanged.
`requote_uri` runs an unquote/quote cycle so the final URL is consistently percent-encoded; an undecodable escape falls back to quoting the whole URI rather than failing.

open_questions.question: The headers about to be attached come from a caller-supplied mapping. What stops a crafted value from turning one request into two?

chapters.title: Headers, Cookies, and the CRLF That Never Happens
chapters.data_out: self.headers = CaseInsensitiveDict with those four validated entries; self._cookies set to the empty jar, no 'Cookie' header added (get_cookie_header returned None)
facts: Every header name and value is matched against a regex before it is stored: names must not start with ':' or whitespace and must contain no CR/LF; values must not start with whitespace and must contain no CR/LF. Failure raises `InvalidHeader` \u2014 this is the request-splitting / header-injection defence, and it runs on *every* request.
A header part that is neither `str` nor `bytes` also raises `InvalidHeader`, so stringification is the caller's job.

`CaseInsensitiveDict` keys on `key.lower()` and keeps the last-written casing \u2014 two headers differing only in case silently collapse into one, which is undefined behaviour by the class's own docstring.

`prepare_cookies` is the only place a `Cookie` header is generated; `MockRequest` adapts the PreparedRequest to the `http.cookiejar` interface so the standard library's domain/path/secure policy governs what is sent, and `is_unverifiable()` always returns True.

The docstring states a one-shot contract: cookielib will not regenerate a `Cookie` header that already exists, so calling `prepare_cookies` twice is a no-op unless the header is deleted first \u2014 redirect handling relies on this by popping 'Cookie' before re-preparing.
A `Host` header set by the caller changes the URL that `MockRequest.get_full_url()` reports, and therefore which cookies match.

open_questions.question: The jar is empty now. If the server sets a cookie, does it survive past this one request?

answers.answer: `check_header_validity` runs on every header pair during preparation and raises `InvalidHeader` on any CR, LF, or leading whitespace, so a value cannot terminate the header block early.

chapters.title: No Body, and the Password Becomes a Header
chapters.data_out: self.body = None (no Content-Length, no Content-Type); headers gain 'Authorization': 'Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz'; hooks {'response': []} registered; PreparedRequest [GET] complete
inputs: empty data, no files, no json
facts: Body precedence is explicit: `json` is only used when `data` is falsy, and `files` overrides plain data by switching to multipart encoding. Passing both `data` and `json` silently drops the `json`.
For GET and HEAD with no body, `prepare_content_length` deliberately omits `Content-Length` entirely; for any other method with no body it sets `Content-Length: 0`.

A file-like or generator body takes the streaming path: if `super_len` can determine a length it sets `Content-Length`, otherwise `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. It records `_body_position` via `tell()` so the body can be rewound on redirect; a failed `tell()` stores a sentinel so a later rewind raises `UnrewindableBodyError` instead of hanging.
Streamed bodies and `files` together raise `NotImplementedError`; invalid JSON (e.g. NaN, since `allow_nan=False`) raises `InvalidJSONError`.
A 2-tuple auth is special-cased into `HTTPBasicAuth`; anything else callable is invoked as-is with the PreparedRequest, which is the extension point for Digest, OAuth and custom schemes.

`_basic_auth_str` encodes username and password as **latin-1** before base64 \u2014 non-latin-1 credentials raise `UnicodeEncodeError`. Non-string credentials are coerced with a `DeprecationWarning` for 3.0.
When `auth is None`, credentials embedded in the URL (`http://user:pass@host/`) are extracted by `get_auth_from_url` and used automatically.
The Authorization header is attached with no regard for the scheme: on this plaintext `http://` URL the base64 credentials go out in clear text, with no warning.

Auth handlers may mutate the request arbitrarily (`self.__dict__.update(r.__dict__)`), so Content-Length is recomputed afterwards, and hooks are prepared last so an auth handler can register response hooks (as HTTPDigestAuth does).

open_questions.question: The credentials are now a header on a plaintext connection. What happens to them if the server answers with a redirect to somewhere else?
There is no body and no Content-Length header. Will the transport interpret that as a chunked request?

answers.answer: In `prepare_auth`: the 2-tuple becomes an `HTTPBasicAuth` instance which is called on the PreparedRequest and sets `Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz` (latin-1 + base64).

chapters.title: What the Environment Gets to Say, and Choosing a Transport
chapters.data_out: {'cert': None, 'proxies': OrderedDict(), 'stream': False, 'verify': True}; adapter = <HTTPAdapter object at 0x10da78190> (the one mounted at 'http://')
facts: Because `trust_env` is True (the default), the process environment can change the security posture of the request: `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` or `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` replaces `verify=True` with a file path, and `http_proxy`/`https_proxy`/`all_proxy` (and uppercase variants) can route the request through a third party.

Environment proxies are only `setdefault`-ed, so an explicit `proxies` argument wins per key; `no_proxy` (argument or env var) can exempt a host, matching plain hostnames, host:port, suffixes, and CIDR ranges for IPv4 literals.
`should_bypass_proxies` temporarily mutates `os.environ['no_proxy']` inside a context manager while calling the platform `proxy_bypass` \u2014 a process-global side effect, restored afterwards.
Setting `trust_env=False` is the only way to make a request fully independent of environment and netrc. Here nothing matched: proxies resolved to empty and verify stayed `True`.

`Session.send` fills in `stream`, `verify`, `cert` defaults and, if `proxies` was not supplied, calls `resolve_proxies` again \u2014 so hooks and redirect resolution always see a complete, reproducible kwargs set.
Passing a `Request` instead of a `PreparedRequest` is explicitly rejected with `ValueError('You can only send PreparedRequests.')`.

`get_adapter` returns the first mounted prefix that the URL *starts with*, case-insensitively; `mount` keeps longer prefixes first. The documented hazard: mounting 'http://localhost' also matches 'http://localhost.evil.com' \u2014 prefixes should end with '/'. No match raises `InvalidSchema`, which is how `mailto:`/`data:` URLs finally fail.
The clock for `Response.elapsed` starts here and stops when headers are parsed, not when the body is read.

open_questions.question: A socket is about to open with `timeout=None`. What, if anything, bounds how long this call can take?

chapters.title: The Adapter: Pools, Certificates, and Everything That Can Go Wrong
chapters.data_in: request=<PreparedRequest [GET]>, stream=False, timeout=None, verify=True, cert=None, proxies=OrderedDict()
chapters.data_out: a live urllib3 HTTPResponse at 0x10c23f910, headers sent as {'User-Agent': ..., 'Authorization': 'Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz'}, url '/basic-auth/user/pass'
facts: The connection-pool key is built from scheme/host/port plus TLS parameters, so connections are never shared across differing `verify`/`cert` settings \u2014 the fix for cross-request TLS confusion.

`cert_verify` is where the TLS guarantee lands: for an `https` URL with `verify` truthy it sets `CERT_REQUIRED` and points at certifi's bundle (or the caller's path/dir), raising `OSError` if the bundle, client cert or key file does not exist. For this plain `http` URL it set `CERT_NONE` and cleared the CA settings \u2014 verification only ever applies to https.
`verify=False` disables certificate *and hostname* checking entirely; it is a one-argument opt-out with no warning from this layer.
`request_url` sends only the path (`/basic-auth/user/pass`); the absolute URL is used only for proxied non-HTTPS requests, and `urldefragauth` strips credentials and fragment from it.
`chunked = not (request.body is None or 'Content-Length' in request.headers)` \u2014 a None body is *not* chunked, so this GET is sent with neither header.
`timeout=None` is passed straight to urllib3 as `TimeoutSauce(connect=None, read=None)`: the request can block indefinitely. A tuple becomes (connect, read); anything else raises `ValueError`.

urllib3 is called with `redirect=False`, `retries=self.max_retries` (0), `preload_content=False` and `decode_content=False`: redirects, retries, body reading and decoding are all Requests' job, not urllib3's.

Every urllib3 failure is translated into a `requests.exceptions` type carrying the request: ProtocolError/OSError \u2192 `ConnectionError`; MaxRetryError \u2192 `ConnectTimeout`/`RetryError`/`ProxyError`/`SSLError`/`ConnectionError` depending on `e.reason`; ReadTimeoutError \u2192 `ReadTimeout`; InvalidHeader \u2192 `InvalidHeader`. Anything unrecognised is re-raised unchanged.
`add_headers` is a documented no-op hook for subclasses; `get_connection` (the pre-2.32.2 API) still exists but emits a `DeprecationWarning`.

open_questions.question: urllib3 handed back a response whose body has not been read and whose connection is still checked out. Who gives it back?

answers.answer: `HTTPAdapter.cert_verify`: for https URLs with the default `verify=True` it sets `CERT_REQUIRED` against certifi's CA bundle; for this http URL it set `CERT_NONE`. Verification only applies to https, and `verify=False` turns it off completely.
No. `chunked` is False when `request.body is None`, so the GET goes out with neither Content-Length nor Transfer-Encoding.
Nothing. `timeout=None` becomes `TimeoutSauce(connect=None, read=None)` and the call can hang indefinitely; with `max_retries=0` there is also no retry budget to cap it.

chapters.title: Dressing the Raw Response
chapters.data_out: <Response [200]> with headers {'Server': ..., 'Content-Type': 'application/json; charset=utf-8', 'Content-Length': '39'}, encoding 'utf-8', url set, cookies jar, request and connection attached
facts: `status_code` is read with `getattr(resp, 'status', None)` \u2014 a Response can legitimately exist with `status_code` None if the transport produced nothing.

Encoding is decided from headers alone: an explicit `charset` wins (here 'utf-8'); otherwise `text/*` falls back to ISO-8859-1 per RFC 2616, `application/json` to utf-8, and anything else leaves `encoding` as None.

Cookies from the server are extracted into `response.cookies` through `MockResponse`, but only if the urllib3 response exposes a non-empty `_original_response`; otherwise extraction silently does nothing.
`response.connection = self` keeps the adapter reachable from the Response \u2014 this is what lets `HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401` resend a request from inside a hook.
At this point the body has not been read: `preload_content=False` means `response.raw` is still a live stream.

open_questions.question: The encoding came from an explicit charset. What would `r.text` have done if the server had not sent one?

chapters.title: Hooks, Cookie Persistence, and the Redirect That Wasn't
chapters.data_out: <Response [200]> unchanged; session jar still empty; get_redirect_target returned None so the redirect generator yields nothing
facts: `dispatch_hook` replaces the response with a hook's return value only if that value is not None; a hook raising an exception propagates to the caller \u2014 hooks must handle their own errors.
Server cookies are copied into the *session* jar here (and for every response in `r.history`), which is what makes cookie persistence a session-level, not request-level, guarantee.
`is_redirect` requires both a `location` header and a status in (301, 302, 303, 307, 308); this 200 matched neither, so `resolve_redirects` produced no responses and `history` stayed empty.

Had it redirected: `rebuild_auth` deletes the `Authorization` header when `should_strip_auth` says the host changed \u2014 same hostname is kept, and http\u2192https on default ports is allowed; `.netrc` may then supply new credentials for the new host if `trust_env`.
`rebuild_proxies` always drops `Proxy-Authorization` and re-derives it, and refuses to re-add it for https targets to avoid leaking it into a tunnel.

Browser-compatibility quirks live in `rebuild_method`: 303 and 302 become GET (except HEAD), and a POST answered with 301 becomes a GET. For non-307/308 redirects the body and Content-Length/Content-Type/Transfer-Encoding headers are dropped.
Exceeding `max_redirects` (30) raises `TooManyRedirects`; each hop consumes the previous body (`resp.content`) before releasing the connection.

open_questions.question: The body is still unread and the socket still open. When does the content actually arrive?

answers.answer: Yes, within this Session: `extract_cookies_to_jar(self.cookies, request, r.raw)` in `Session.send` copies server cookies into the session jar \u2014 but this Session is discarded at the end of `requests.get`.

On a redirect, `rebuild_auth` strips the `Authorization` header whenever `should_strip_auth` detects a different hostname (or a port/scheme change other than http\u2192https on default ports); same-host redirects keep the credentials.

chapters.title: Reading the Body, Closing Everything, and Decoding What Came Back
chapters.data_in: <Response [200]> with stream=False and an unread raw stream
chapters.data_out: r._content = b'{"authenticated": true, "user": "user"}'; Session closed; 'application/json; charset=utf-8', 'utf-8', '{"authenticated": true, "user": "user"}', {'authenticated': True, 'user': 'user'}
facts: Because `stream` is False, `Session.send` touches `r.content` before returning: the body is fully read into memory and the connection goes back to the pool automatically. With `stream=True` that is the caller's responsibility, and an unread response holds a pooled connection.

`content` caches into `_content`, so repeated access is free; reading it twice from a streamed, already-consumed response raises `StreamConsumedError`, and a second attempt after consumption raises `RuntimeError`.

`iter_content` translates transport failures mid-body into Requests exceptions: ProtocolError \u2192 `ChunkedEncodingError`, DecodeError \u2192 `ContentDecodingError`, ReadTimeoutError \u2192 `ConnectionError`, SSLError \u2192 `requests.exceptions.SSLError`. These can surface *after* a 200 status was already observed.

`Session.close` (fired by `__exit__`) clears every adapter's PoolManager and any ProxyManagers, so the per-call Session leaves no sockets behind \u2014 at the cost of no keep-alive reuse between top-level `requests.get` calls, which is exactly why Sessions exist as a public API.
`r.headers['content-type']` works in any casing because response headers live in a `CaseInsensitiveDict`.

`text` decodes with `errors='replace'` and falls back to a bare `str(content, errors='replace')` on `LookupError`/`TypeError` \u2014 it never raises for bad bytes or a bogus charset, it silently substitutes replacement characters.

When no encoding came from the headers, `text` falls back to `apparent_encoding`, i.e. charset_normalizer/chardet statistical detection (or plain 'utf-8' if neither library is installed) \u2014 a guess, not a guarantee.

`json()` is not cached: the trace shows it re-decoding the text on each of the two calls. It uses `guess_json_utf` only when `encoding` is unset, and wraps decode failures as `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError`.

Nothing in this path checks the status code. A 404 or 500 returns a perfectly ordinary Response with parseable JSON; `raise_for_status()` is opt-in, and truthiness of a Response (`bool(r)`) is just `status_code < 400`.

answers.answer: The per-call Session guarantees no leaked sockets (`__exit__` \u2192 `close()` clears all pools) but forfeits keep-alive, connection pooling and cookie persistence across calls \u2014 reuse `requests.Session()` when making several requests to the same host.
`Session.send` itself: with `stream=False` it accesses `r.content`, which drains `raw` and lets urllib3 return the connection to the pool; `Session.close` then clears the pools entirely.

With no charset in the Content-Type, `encoding` would be ISO-8859-1 for `text/*`, utf-8 for `application/json`, and otherwise None \u2014 in which case `text` falls back to `apparent_encoding`, a charset_normalizer/chardet guess.

Right here, inside `Session.send`: because `stream=False`, `r.content` runs `iter_content` to completion, caching the bytes and releasing the connection before the Response is handed back to the caller.
